content.thinking:
I'm planning the kraken design to write in one pass: a large domed mantle with eyes rising from water, and eight tentacles spreading outward and down to touch the floor at y=0, sized roughly 3m mantle with 6m tentacle spread for a dramatic scale.

For the visual style I'm going with bold Overwatch-inspired shapes with clean panel lines and a strong accent color — deep indigo-blue body with dark steel-teal armor plates and glowing cyan accents on the suckers and eyes, keeping colors flat to avoid risky paint APIs on glow elements.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure: a root joint for the mantle base, a spine chain running up through the body for the loft shape, and tentacles radiating outward from the base joint.

I'm also planning the environment — a water surface as a flattened lathe disc with a foam ring and splash droplets, positioned so the tentacle tips just touch the surface without sinking too far below it. For the eight tentacles, I'm working out how to distribute them evenly around the core at staggered azimuth angles, each arcing outward and upward before curving back down to the floor.

I'm defining each tentacle's path as a sequence of control points moving from near the core outward and down to the floor, with varying radial lengths so tentacles don't look uniform, and tapering the sweep radius from thick near the body down to a thin curled tip resting just above the water surface.

For dynamism I'll raise two of the tentacles upward in a curling arc rather than resting flat, pushing the overall silhouette height to around 5, while keeping the mantle itself closer to 4.2 so the raised tentacles read as an active flourish rather than bloating the whole creature's scale.

Each tentacle gets built as its own chain of six joints following a catmull-rom curve off the core, with unique auto-generated joint names, then swept with a tapering radius function that's thick near the base and thins toward the tip, colored with a countershading scheme that's lighter on top.

For the belly markings I'm thinking of using sector regions on the underside to suggest suckers with a cream color, while keeping the main body color using a mottled paint pattern for a more organic texture rather than flat fills.

Still working out the suckers: I need to loop along the tentacle's length on the belly side, placing small sucker discs at each point with radius tapering from wide near the base to narrow at the tip.

Setting glow effects on the sucker discs and designing the armor plate bands along the mantle, defining spine joint positions to create the tilted-back chain structure for the mantle plates.

Tuning the radius profile along the mantle...

Now I'm shaping the head core sphere with cel-shaded mottling, then working out the beak as a jointed upper and lower jaw structure positioned at the center-bottom of the tentacle mass.

I'm checking the head sphere's geometry so the beak sits slightly tucked at the front-bottom without poking too far out. For the eyes, I'm thinking of a sci-fi look with dark sockets and glowing centers rather than a typical anime eye style.

Now I'm settling on cyan as the single accent color for glowing suckers, rune lines, and the eyes, with a cephalopod-style horizontal slit pupil set against a glowing sphere eyeball, framed by armored brow ridges. Positioning the eyeball and dark pupil ellipsoid...

Still defining facial geometry...

Adding fin paint pattern...

Now thinking about armor plates around the mantle using sweep loops at the joints, though I'm wary the loop operation might fail if the cutting plane doesn't cleanly intersect the mantle geometry or the head sphere.

Adding rivet studs along each loop with small brass spheres, then dorsal ridge spikes along the mantle sweep for the armored texture.

For the mantle markings, I'm drawing glowing rune-like stripes along diagonal lines across the sweep surface, lifting them slightly off the plate geometry to avoid intersection clipping.

Now I'm thinking through tentacle details, adding armor cuff bands near the thick base of each tentacle by looping around the sweep at a fixed parameter point, though curving tentacles risk the cutting plane intersecting the surface more than once.

Defining the color palette now — indigo skin tones with lighter spot accents and darker shading, plus a shared paint function so markings stay consistent across mantle, head, and tentacles.

Settling on a cream-colored belly for warmth against the cyan glow, with crisp off-white armor plates trimmed in dark gunmetal and indigo for an Overwatch-style contrast, and a dark beak to finish the face.

For the water I'm picking a deeper blue tone with light foam highlights so it doesn't clash with the cyan accents, and I'm considering adding a helmet-like armor crest on top of the head using a hemisphere cap geometry to cover the top-back section.

Now I'm working out a visor band across the brow between the eyes, calculating the curved ellipsoid surface positions at different head heights to figure out where the face plate geometry should sit relative to the eye sockets.

Solving for eye center coordinates on the head surface, I get roughly (±0.62, 1.95, 0.95) with eyeball radius 0.27 partially embedded, then computing the outward normal direction so the eyes face slightly upward rather than straight out.

I'm trying to figure out a crest or crown structure for the top of the head, considering armored plates or a dorsal ridge fin between head and mantle, but the geometry feels too risky and float-prone — I'll skip the custom crest outline and just use simple dorsal spikes instead.

Now I'm adding a forehead cap piece using a partial sphere oriented along a forward-upward direction, with non-uniform scaling to approximate the right curvature over the skull.

Checking the eye position against that 35° angle, it's too close to the cap edge, so I retilt the cap axis upward and back, which pushes the eye angle out to 43° — safely outside the 36° cap boundary. With the cap centered higher and radius 1.1, it clears the eyes while still covering the top of the head.

Now I'm checking the gap between the cap surface and the head surface at different angles to find the right scale factor — too loose a fit looks like it's floating, too tight and it clips the head. Settling on a uniform scale of 0.97 gives a snug fit at both the pole and the 36° edge, so I'll use that and add a trim ring around the rim.

I'm placing a thin glowing cyan torus right at the cap's edge for an accent detail, computing its radius and position from the cap's cone angle. Then I'm sketching the base water disc using a lathe profile, defining its outline points before moving on.

For the water level, I need the surface high enough that tentacle tips actually dip beneath it rather than floating above the floor—so I'm adjusting the disc's top and bottom y-values so the water reads as a real surface the tentacles emerge from and touch.

Shaping the ripple rings and foam torus outlines...

Rethinking the body's connection to the water: rather than floating the head mid-air, I should have the tentacles arc down and support it tripod-style, or add a webbed mantle skirt that extends from the head down to the surface, filling that gap visually.

I'll give the stem joints a "spine" role, then rework the core coordinates: core at [0,1.7,0], head sphere centered at (0,2.0,0.3) with radii (1.05,0.85,1.0), eyes offset to y=2.35, beak positioned below and in front, and the mantle sitting behind the head.

I'm plotting the mantle curving up and back from the head, ending with a tall, flared top that brings the total height to roughly 5 meters, then scaling the whole kraken up so its tentacle span reaches about 12 meters across. I'm also defining the stem chain running down from the core to the base, with tentacles branching off a ring positioned partway down that stem.

Now I'm setting the tentacles to parent off the lower stem joint, and thinking through how to shade the stem — gradient from skin tone at the top toward a lighter belly tone, possibly with decorative banding loops along its length.

I'm working out the tentacle base positions and sweeping each one outward from center along a radial direction, plotting a path that rises, arcs to an apex, then descends back down toward the ground.

Checking the radius formula stays within the height limit, I'll clamp the tip offset to around 0.08 for safety. I'm also setting up varied tentacle curl styles and radii, with azimuth angles spaced at 45-degree intervals around the body to position front-facing and raised tentacles distinctly.

Picking i=2 and i=5 as the raised side tentacles, I'm plotting their curling path coordinates so they arc upward and inward, keeping total height near 6.8m while the others stay grounded to maintain balance and proper framing.

I'm now setting up the sweep logic for each tentacle chain—resampling ground tentacles with fewer points and raised ones with more for smoother curls—then building radius functions so thickness tapers proportionally along each chain, with base tentacle thickness around 0.42 against a stem radius of 0.8.

I should bump the stem radius to 0.95 and adjust the starting point radius so the tentacle base sits snugly inside the stem without a visible seam, then figure out belly paint sectors and alternating sucker row angles along each tentacle's length.

Now I'm working out the sucker geometry: scaling disc radius as a function of position along the tube, layering a glowing inner cylinder inside a slightly larger outer cylinder, and sinking each piece into the tentacle surface by an embed fraction of its height so they look attached rather than floating.

With 11 suckers per tentacle across 8 tentacles, I'm placing them spaced from t=0.12 to 0.92, giving cream-colored discs with cyan glowing centers to match the accent palette. I'm also planning belly-color sectors, a cel-shaded top pattern, and tentacle tip caps, plus armor plates near the tentacle bases using simple ring/box shapes.

Adding armor bands with rivets around each ring, plus mantle plates and other decorative elements, pushing the total part count toward roughly 460 and keeping the triangle budget under 60k by using low-poly cylinders and spheres for the small repeated pieces like suckers and rivets.

Now I'm double-checking the API signatures I'm relying on — sweep radius functions, sector fill types, chain-based sweep attachment points, stick embedding on sweep frames, and the glow import — to make sure each call matches the expected argument shapes before I finalize the code.

I'm also checking the loop placement logic: `chain.at(0.1)` should return a frame at that point along the tentacle curve, and since each tentacle's plane only intersects its own geometry near the base, there shouldn't be a "plane misses" error, so I can safely sweep a small-radius loop path for the armor ring.

For rivets, I'm scattering sphere studs along the loop using the `along` helper, which samples points evenly across the path and lets me place a part at each one.

To get rivets sitting on the crest of the band rather than inside it, I need a second loop at a higher lift value—around 0.1—so the studs sit outward on the ring surface rather than embedded in it.

Now I'm sketching the mantle rivets similarly, then moving to the beak: sweeping a quadratic bezier curve with a tapering radius from 0.2 down to 0.02, flat at the base and pointed at the tip, colored and bound to the core bone. For the jaw, I'm adding a joint parented to the core, positioned and aimed to form a hinge, with the lower beak bone attached to it, while the upper beak curves out from inside the head.

I'm positioning the control points for the upper beak's curve so it hooks downward and overlaps the lower beak's tip, adjusting their y and z coordinates until the upper beak sits in front and the lower stays tucked behind, with radii tapering from 0.2/0.17 down to 0.02.

I'm flattening the beak cross-section to a wide, shallow ellipse instead of a round tube, then checking where the beak origin sits relative to the head sphere's surface at different heights so it emerges naturally without poking through awkwardly. Now I'm setting up the jaw joint attachment point on the skull.

I'll skip the dark mouth hollow detail for now. Setting up the core as the root joint with no parent, then building the mantle chain off it using a catmull spline through a few points above the core.

Checking the curve: it starts inside the head volume with a wide radius around 0.95-1.05, then tapers down to a pointed tip at 0.12 near the top, giving it a natural flop toward the back.

Now I'm working out the fins—attaching them at a point further along the mantle chain, angled outward and back-up, and sketching the fin outline shape as a polygon that flares wide then narrows toward the tip.

Normalizing the fin's axis vectors, then setting up a flat paint function for the fin color with a cel shading wrapper and white armor ridge edges. For the mantle, I'm sweeping along the dorsal line to place armored spikes outward from the body.

Actually I realize the dorsal reference, since the tube tilts backward, points toward the front-up side rather than the rear — and I want spikes on the belly/rear side instead, so I'm switching the angle to 180° to place the spikes pointing backward along the rear of the mantle.

I'm looping through 6 decreasing-sized spikes along the mantle crest, then adding glowing cyan side lines following the sweep path (trimmed to avoid the head area), and starting to lathe an outline for the water disc shape.

For the water, I'm making sure its radius is wide enough to contain the tentacle tips, setting it to 7.4 so nothing extends past the surface, and attaching the water mesh rigidly to the core bone so it stays positioned correctly relative to the rest of the body.

Now I'm adding mottled blue coloring for the water and layering in ripple rings around specific radii, plus trapezoid-shaped foam outlines lathed around the Y axis to simulate surface foam, including small foam rings at each point where a tentacle tip touches the water.

Still refining foam ring geometry...

Now I'm planning scattered water droplets as tiny spheres near the stem base, randomly positioned around a given radius range.

For the eye, I'm building a glowing cyan eyeball with a dark pupil slit and a torus-shaped socket rim in dark armor color, plus brow rods connecting outer and inner points for added detail.

I'm checking the brow rod endpoints against the head's surface equation, since one outer point lands outside the head boundary and floats awkwardly, so I need to shift it inward to a position that actually sits on the head's surface.

Rather than hand-computing head-surface math for each feature, it's simpler to use a surface-hit function that casts around the head at given azimuth/elevation angles to place the eyes and brow points directly on the skin, then build the brow as a smooth curve through several of these hit points swept with a small radius.

Working out pupil orientation...

Rather than resolving the exact embed geometry, I decide to place the eye explicitly: eye origin at the hit point plus a small offset along the normal, with the cylinder axis aligned to the normal so its default local-X stays roughly horizontal, giving a horizontal slit shape scaled thin in one axis and short in depth, then positioned slightly outward so the pupil sits just above the surface.

I'll write a small offset helper that moves a point along a hit's normal by a given distance, then use it to place the eye sphere and pupil cylinder relative to the hit frame, and add a tiny white sphere for the pupil highlight.

Skipping the highlight for now since computing a tangent offset is fiddly, and instead adding a thin armor-colored torus ring around the eye socket, positioned using the hit's axis direction. Then I'm shaping the head sphere itself, scaling it to be wider and flatter to read as a face base.

Head cap placement looks right relative to the scaled head ellipsoid, and the mantle origin lines up cleanly with the head center. I'll skip adding feeler tentacles for now, but I'll add a glowing cyan accent ring along the head cap edge as a decorative marking, and consider segmented plate armor across the mantle instead of just simple rings.

Adding a tapered central armor spine strip along the mantle's front, swept with a radius that narrows from base to tip, colored in gunmetal with rivet accents, plus thin glow lines flanking it on either side.

I'm checking the type declarations for the sector array, making sure the tuple shape of angle ranges and fill colors is properly typed as a readonly array so TypeScript accepts it, and double-checking that only actually-used imports remain to avoid unused-import errors.

Now I'm working through the tentacle coloring logic—layering spot paint over the base skin tone with seeded randomness for droplet effects, then verifying each import (catmull, bezier, glow, cel, paint, spots, mottle, rng) is actually used somewhere in the final code.

For the armor cuff geometry, I'm computing tube radius at specific points along the tentacle and considering whether to use a thin ring or a wider swept band with rivets, while double-checking that cutting the loop plane through a curved tentacle still picks the correct nearby loop rather than a distant one on a spiral path.

Beyond the stem decoration rings, I'm now thinking about adding webbing membranes between adjacent tentacle bases—slicing each tentacle's path near the root and connecting pairs with a thin membrane surface to give it a more organic, webbed-arm look, binding each web segment to the nearest stem bone.

I'll define each web edge using a point along the arm's path capped at roughly 2.2m arc length, draping cream-colored membranes between adjacent arm centerlines at a thin thickness. Webs between ground arms and the raised arms (i=1,2) still span reasonably at that length, so I'll accept that pairing and move on to limiting which arm pairs actually get webs.

I'll only connect adjacent pairs where neither arm is raised, giving four membranes total: (0,1), (3,4), (6,7), and (7,0), each defined by matching path edges and a shared bone joint from the stem. For the raised arms, I'm adding a small glowing cyan orb at the tip instead, which should read better against the high camera angle, and I'll extend that luminous tip treatment to the curled arm tips as well.

For the ground arms, I'm working out the tip position above water and attaching the glow orb to the last joint in the bone chain, falling back to the final joint index if a named tip isn't available. Writing the path function for ground arm positions, computing radial and tangential offsets to build each arm's curve with proper perpendicular direction vectors.

Now I'm checking the catmull-centripetal curve through the ground arm control points, verifying the sweep height stays above the water surface even with the slight overshoot near the tip segments -- the dip looks small enough to stay within tolerance.

For the raised arms, I'm defining the sweep radius variation across ground arms and the forward-facing placement of the tentacles, then laying out the control-point path for a raised arm's curve as it extends away from the mantle.

I'll tone down the overall height slightly and simplify the vertical path to 6 key points, then set up the chain structure with consistent joint counts and bone naming across all tentacles.

Still writing sucker placement logic...

I'm picking chain points at several t-values for ring placement, checking radius scaling along the mantle taper. Now I'm sketching the fin outline as a set of typed points with sharp corners for the extrude function.

I'm positioning the fin root at the midpoint of the mantle chain, offsetting it along x and y so it sits embedded at the correct radius and extends outward.

For the fin's coloring, I'm giving it a dark indigo base with thin cyan-ish ray stripes using a paint callback, and I'm planning to add six armor spikes along the rear dorsal crest.

Deciding to skip belly plate color sectors and eyelid details since the stem skin is already smooth and fins ride the mantle fine. For the water lathe shape, I'm bumping segments up to 28 for a smoother disc and foam ring, with a 10-segment ring at the tentacle tip, using a mottled cel paint for the water surface.

I'm positioning the foam rings and water lathe centered near the stem's z-offset, working out radii so the water disc covers the tentacle reach, and checking that the front and side tentacle arm positions stay within the water's bounds given their angle and extension.

Now I'm setting up the foam ring lathe call with appropriate offset, color, and segment count, then planning how to compute tentacle foam positions from the parametric P(a,R,...) coordinates before scattering some droplets.

Then I'm randomizing droplet spheres with varying radius, angle, height, and size, coloring them foam, and double-checking the flat color palette versus textured skin shading to keep the overall palette count manageable before defining the base skin color and its spot variations for the cel-shaded material.

Adding glow line paths...

Still building the kraken rig...

Adding mantle chain and sweep...

For the head I'm placing a sphere at a fixed anchor point, then overlaying a partial sphere cap angled slightly forward as a helmet shell, open at the edge so the inside faces show through as a thin hollow rim.

I'm covering that open rim with a thin cyan-glowing torus positioned and scaled to exactly match the cap's opening angle, then considering a few small spikes on top as a crest but deciding to simplify to a single ridge.

Now I'm computing the two side horns by rotating around the cap's tangent axis to find symmetric edge points, then placing spike geometry angled outward and slightly downward from each.

Next I'm positioning the eyes using a spherical surface helper that samples the head's outer surface at given azimuth and elevation angles, confirming the up-angle matches my earlier estimate of roughly 20 degrees.

I check the math and confirm the eye azimuth comes out to about 43°, matching my earlier estimate. But comparing the eye direction to the helmet cap's edge, the eye sphere actually overlaps the cap boundary slightly, so I need to shrink the cap angle to about 29° and redo the rim torus trig to clear it properly.

Working out the torus position and radius with the new cap angle, then placing the horn bases symmetrically on either side. I decide to try lowering the eye elevation slightly and adjusting azimuth instead, settling on elevation 12.

Now I'm sketching the eyeball part: a cyan sphere attached to the core bone at the offset position, with a glow effect layered on top, followed by a socket torus to frame it.

I'm working out where the socket ring should sit relative to the eyeball's radius so it wraps around the equator without clipping, then moving on to sketch the brow geometry using surface hit points at varying azimuth and elevation values, checking whether Frame objects can be used directly as points for the catmull curve.

Now I'm checking the angular spacing between brow and eye so they don't overlap, then starting the beak sweep using a bezier curve through three control points with a tapering width profile.

Sorting out the radius function's type—whether it returns a tuple or a number array—then starting the lower beak curve's bezier control points.

I'm also adding a dark sphere inside the head to suggest the mouth gap between the beaks, and noting that webbing geometry needs to reuse the same path objects as the arm chains rather than redefining them.

Now I'm writing the loop that builds each of the eight tentacle arms, computing control points per arm with alternating raised poses, converting them into Catmull-Rom paths, and spawning a joint chain parented to the stem's first joint for each one. I'm also starting on a radius function to taper the tentacle thickness along its length.

Adding sucker rivets and armor bands...

To be safe I'll just create fresh geometry each time rather than share it across meshes with different transforms. I'm checking that rivet placement sits right at the ring crest, adding a glowing tip orb at the final chain joint, and setting up ground foam positioning for arms that aren't raised.

Now I'm defining the web membranes connecting adjacent arm pairs, choosing edge slices that run root-to-tip and verifying the adjacency wraps correctly around the last pair back to the first. I'm picking a light lavender translucent color for the webbing and attaching it to the stem's base joint with a thin thickness setting.

Then I'm working on the mantle rear spikes, looping through six positions along the dorsal arc with decreasing height and width, sampling points from the mantle's silhouette curve, and coloring them with the armor tone.

Next I'm adding a tapered armor strip down the mantle's front face, checking that the dorsal reference angle lines up with the correct side given the mantle's tilt. I'll skip rivets and gem details on the strip for now, and start sketching glow rune lines along the sides.

Now I'm finishing the model with droplet/water texture details, metadata (name, description, style, commit hash), and returning the final builder root. I'm also double-checking that all imports (THREE, OutlinePoint, createBuilder, offset, rng, bezier, catmull, mottle, paint, spots, cel, glow) are actually used, and starting to define the fin's cel-shaded paint pattern based on angular banding.

Now I'm writing the fin extrusion calls on both sides of the mantle, then defining foam ring outline shapes for the tentacle tips using small quadrilateral loops colored with the foam texture.

I'm checking height bounds against the water surface, then generating random foam droplets scattered around the core using a seeded RNG to control angle, radius, and size for each sphere.

Now I'm writing the sucker geometry along the tentacle, alternating positions at fixed intervals and angles, pairing a base ring cylinder with a glowing cyan inner ring for each sucker. Just double-checking the glow intensity and variable naming before finalizing the file.
